record.question:
A company exposes an HTTPS application through CloudFront and an ALB. It needs managed mitigation and resource-level notifications for network and transport-layer DDoS events, including SYN floods and UDP reflection. It also needs configurable HTTP inspection rules for SQL injection and cross-site scripting. The company has approved the required protection subscription.

Which actions meet these requirements together? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable Shield Advanced protection for the eligible public resources. Configure CloudWatch alarms for relevant Shield detection metrics and send notifications through SNS.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the application entry point and configure tested SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and application-specific request rules.
Configure SNS notifications from an ALB request-count alarm and increase the Auto Scaling maximum capacity to handle traffic spikes.
Increase the CloudFront cache hit ratio and rely only on the automatically included Shield Standard protection, without configuring attack-notification metrics or HTTP inspection rules.
Route outbound VPC traffic through Network Firewall and configure an allowlist of external domains that application instances may contact.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<2>> are correct. Shield Advanced provides enhanced protection and detection metrics for protected resources; CloudWatch and SNS turn those signals into notifications. WAF examines HTTP request components for application-layer attack patterns, including SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

<<3>> observes completed HTTP requests reaching the ALB. It neither identifies every network-layer flood nor supplies the requested mitigation and content inspection.

<<4>> provides useful edge capacity and baseline DDoS protection but omits the stated notification and HTTP-rule controls.

<<5>> controls outbound destinations, not the required public-entry threat path. Network Firewall is a VPC traffic inspection service and can be useful in a single VPC; it is not limited to multi-account governance.

Tune alarms and WAF rules against normal traffic and investigation needs. A DDoS detection metric warrants investigation, and filtering does not remove the need to fix vulnerable application code.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Shield Advanced metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/shield-metrics.html). [Shield alerts with SNS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-get-started-create-alarms.html). [WAF SQL injection rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-sqli-match.html). [WAF cross-site scripting rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-xss-match.html). [Network Firewall scope](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-firewall/latest/developerguide/what-is-aws-network-firewall.html).

diagram_alt: A comparison maps network-layer mitigation, event notification, HTTP inspection, and outbound filtering to their distinct control paths.

sources.supports: Protected-resource detection metrics including DDoSDetected and layer 3/4 attack-volume metrics
CloudWatch alarms and SNS notification configuration
Inspection of malicious SQL in HTTP request components
Inspection of malicious scripts in HTTP request components
Managed stateful VPC traffic inspection distinct from Firewall Manager governance

editorial_notes: Preserved answer set 1 and 2. Added explicit alarm-to-SNS configuration and corrected the Network Firewall versus Firewall Manager confusion.
